coltrane.cycleOrder: The key order of Coltrane's cycle (“Giant Steps”) is:

e-string-notes.name: Notes of the E string
e-string-notes.theory: Improvisation starts with knowing the fretboard. We begin with the low E string: the notes run chromatically E F F# G G# A A# B C C# D D# E in frets 0–12. Once you know it by heart, half of the fretboard map is done — the A string repeats the same layout shifted up 5 semitones. Practice both directions: see a position and name the note, then read a name and find it on the neck.

key-signatures.name: Key Signatures
key-signatures.theory: A key tells you which notes “live at home”. The circle of fifths orders the keys: moving clockwise adds sharps (C→G→D→A→E→B), counter-clockwise adds flats (C→F→Bb→Eb→Ab). The number of accidentals in the key signature is the fastest way to recognize a key on paper. When a bandmate says “play in D”, the key signature is what makes that unambiguous.

pentatonic-scale.name: Pentatonic Scale
pentatonic-scale.theory: The minor pentatonic (1 b3 4 5 b7) is most players' first improvising vocabulary — it works over blues, rock and folk. The standard box (e.g. A in frets 5–8) sits comfortably under the fingers and teaches phrasing inside one position instead of running all over the neck. Switching keys C/A/D/E/G teaches transposing the shape rather than memorizing random frets. Play full runs up and down with a metronome so your timing stays even.

major-scale.name: Major Scale
major-scale.theory: The major scale (1 2 3 4 5 6 7) is the reference point for everything that follows — modes, chord construction and harmony analysis are all counted against it. A one-position box (three notes per string) lays the whole pattern out where you can see it. Practice up and down with a metronome, then in thirds and fourths — that is how a scale turns into melodic material.

fretboard-notes.name: Notes of the Rest of the Fretboard
fretboard-notes.term: Notes of the Rest of the Fretboard
fretboard-notes.theory: Now we extend the map to all strings. The key: neighbouring strings E–A–D–G are a perfect fourth apart (5 semitones), and G–B a major third (4 semitones). If you know the E and A strings, you can derive the rest upwards. The goal is to see every note anywhere in frets 0–12; without it, following the changes higher up the neck is guesswork.

pentatonic-positions.name: Pentatonic Scale Positions
pentatonic-positions.theory: These five boxes are one scale: G minor pentatonic (G, Bb, C, D, F) spread across the neck. Each box starts on the next degree of that pentatonic, and each box is named after the chord its starting note serves: G minor pent (3fr), Bb major pent (5fr), C dorian pent (7fr), D phrygian pent (10fr), F mixo pent (12fr). Same five notes in every box — what changes is which note feels like home. Own each box, then connect them.

modes.name: Modes
modes.theory: Modes are the seven rotations of the major scale: I Ionian, II Dorian, III Phrygian, IV Lydian, V Mixolydian, VI Aeolian, VII Locrian. Relative to major: Dorian = b3 b7, Phrygian = b2, Lydian = #4, Mixolydian = b7, Aeolian = b3 b6 b7, Locrian = b2 b3 b5 b6 b7. Learn the W/H pattern and train your ear on the characteristic note: Lydian is all about #4, Mixolydian about b7, Phrygian about b2.

chord-construction.name: How Chords Are Built
chord-construction.theory: Chords come from the scale: stack every other note (1-3-5) from a scale degree. In F major: F-A-C is degree I (major), G-Bb-D is ii (minor), E-G-Bb is vii (diminished). You recognize a triad type by its distances: major third + perfect fifth = major, minor third + perfect fifth = minor, minor third + diminished fifth = dim, major third + augmented fifth = aug. The same stacking extends to seventh chords and every extension used in improvisation.

chord-scale-major.name: Chord/Scale Relationships (Major)
chord-scale-major.theory: Every diatonic chord has “its” scale: Dm7 → Dorian (Dm13 is the same world with extensions), Em7 → Phrygian, Fmaj7 → Lydian (hence the characteristic #11), G7 → Mixolydian, Am7 → Aeolian, Bm7b5 → Locrian. In practice: play the key's scale but aim at the chord's characteristic tones. This is the first step from “playing the key” to “following the changes”.

triads.name: Triads
triads.theory: Triads on the top three strings (G-B-E) are the economical way to see harmony: one shape, a subset of the chord, with its inversions sitting right next to each other on the neck. Knowing them you can comp and see melodic target notes at the same time. Also drill the names → intervals: major 1 3 5, minor 1 b3 5, diminished 1 b3 b5, augmented 1 3 #5 — without this the harmony quizzes become guessing.

arpeggios.name: Arpeggios
arpeggios.theory: An arpeggio is a chord played note by note — the “safest” material over changing chords because it contains only notes that fit. The seventh-chord shape (1 3 5 b7 for dom7, 1 b3 5 b7 for m7) spread one note per string (E-A-D-G) shows the whole chord structure inside one position. In improvisation the arpeggio steers the line: scales, chromatics and approach notes hang off this skeleton.

target-chord-tones.name: How to Target Chord Tones
target-chord-tones.theory: “Following the changes” starts with landing on chord tones exactly when the chord changes. Over Am–C–Em–D aim at the third (C, E, G, F#) or the fifth (E, G, B, A) of each chord — the third defines the major/minor colour, the fifth is stable and safe. Take the approach note from the previous chord; the landing is new. That contrast carries the line.

voice-leading.name: Voice Leading
voice-leading.theory: Voice leading means minimal movement between chords: find the common tone or a half/whole step away from a note of the next chord. Gm→Bbm shares Bb, Gm→Cm shares G — play that note right before the change and your line glides through the harmony instead of jumping. The same rule drives comping: move by 1–2 frets instead of teleporting across the neck.

switching-keys.name: How to Switch Keys While Improvising
switching-keys.term: How to Switch Keys While Improvising
switching-keys.theory: Modulating while improvising: find a chord shared by both keys (pivot chord) or use a ii–V to “announce” the new key. In the drill the key changes halfway through the loop (G → B): your material — pentatonics, scales, arpeggios — must move with it. Train it deliberately: hear the change first, then pick your shape in the new key, finally connect both worlds with one line.

tritone-subs.name: Tritone Substitutions
tritone-subs.theory: Tritone substitution: replace a dominant with the dominant a tritone above — G7 → Db7. Both chords share the same tritone (third and seventh swap places), so they serve the same function, but the bass now moves chromatically: Dm7–Db7–C instead of Dm7–G7–C. Emphasize the subV's third and b7 and resolve them stepwise — the classic jazz descending-bass tension and release.

secondary-dominants.name: Secondary Dominants
secondary-dominants.theory: A secondary dominant is the V7 of a chord's “temporary” key: A7 leads to Dm7 (V7/ii), B7 to Em7, C7 to Fmaj7, D7 to G7, E7 to Am7. They inject tension and motion inside one key without changing it for good. The progression C–A7–Dm7–G7–C shows the mechanism: each dominant aims at the target chord's tones — the third works best.

borrowed-chords.name: Borrowed Chords
borrowed-chords.theory: Borrowed chords come from the parallel minor key: bVII7 (Bb7 in C), iv m (Fm), bVI (Ab), bIII (Eb). The most famous case is the backdoor ii–V: Fm7–Bb7→C. Over Fm7 play F dorian; over Bb7 play Bb Lydian dominant (or plain Bb mixolydian). The Bb root rises a whole step into C — that whole-step rise is the backdoor sound.

melodic-minor.name: Melodic Minor Scale and Modes
melodic-minor.theory: Melodic minor (1 2 b3 4 5 6 7) is “the jazz scale”: minor on the bottom, major on top — a smooth sound without the harmonic-minor gap. It is more useful for improvisation than harmonic minor because its modes cover m(Maj7), 7alt, Lydian Dominant and a whole family of modern sounds. Own the A box around fret 4, then move the shape to other keys with the switcher.

chord-scale-melodic.name: Melodic Minor Chord/Scale Relationships
chord-scale-melodic.theory: The melodic minor modes pair with chords: I Melodic Minor → m(Maj7), II Dorian b2 → m7, III Lydian Augmented → Maj7#5, IV Lydian Dominant → 7(#11), V Mixolydian b6 → 7(b13), VI Aeolian b5 → m7b5, VII Altered → 7alt. (Some players also use Altered over m7b5; the standard pairing is 7alt.) Recognize the chord symbol and you know which scale supplies its “jazz” colour.

harmonic-minor.name: Harmonic Minor Scale and Modes
harmonic-minor.theory: Harmonic minor (1 2 b3 4 5 b6 7) has the distinctive b6→7 leap — instantly recognizable. It sits near the end of the learning order not because it is hard, but because it matters less for improvisation than everything before it. Still, its fifth mode (Phrygian Dominant) and its intervals come up often — own the C box around fret 6, then move it to other keys.

chord-scale-harmonic.name: Harmonic Minor Chord/Scale Relationships
chord-scale-harmonic.theory: The harmonic minor modes pair with chords: I Harmonic Minor → m(Maj7), II Locrian #6 → m7b5, III Ionian #5 → Maj7#5, IV Dorian #4 → m7. Next: V Phrygian Dominant → 7, VI Lydian #2 → Maj7, VII Superlocrian bb7 → dim7. In practice you will use Phrygian Dominant over a dominant heading to a minor chord (V7/x in minor) and the scale itself over m(Maj7) most often.

giant-steps.name: Giant Steps
giant-steps.theory: Coltrane's “Giant Steps” is the final boss: keys in major-third triangles (B–G–Eb), the progression |Bmaj7 D7|Gmaj7 Bb7|Ebmaj7 F#7|Bmaj7|. The dominants (D7, Bb7, F#7) resolve down a fifth into the “next” key every two chords, and the key changes faster than in any standard. Play chord thirds (arpeggios) through the changes and slow down to 60 BPM — once this is yours, the whole earlier list clicks into one system.
